list.listitem: Use a validated clinical rule like the Wells score for an estimation of the pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) to assist with the diagnostic process.A
Compression ultrasonography is the best initial imaging test for detecting clinically significant DVT.A
A normal D-dimer test in a low-risk patient rules out DVT.A

For acute DVT, treat patients with one of the new oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban). If choosing warfarin, dabigatran, or edoxaban, bridge with unfractionated heparin (UFH) or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for at least 5 days; for warfarin, discontinue heparin when the INR has stabilized between 2 and 3.A
Initial outpatient treatment of DVT with LMWH is an option for clinically stable patients with adequate follow-up.A

For patients with acute isolated distal DVT, the ACCP guidelines recommend 2 weeks of serial imaging, with anticoagulation only if it extends or if the patient has severe symptoms or risk factors for extension.A

DVT is a partial or total thrombotic occlusion of the deep venous system, most often of the legs. DVT and pulmonary embolism (PE) are both components of the clinical presentation of venous thromboembolism (VTE).
100 episodes/100,000 persons/y.
An estimated 900,000 VTE cases (DVT or PE) occur annually and account for up to 300,000 deaths.
Without prophylaxis, the incidence of hospital-acquired DVT in medical or general surgical patients is 10% to 40% and is even higher after major orthopedic surgery.
High costs are associated with both the initial event and the long-term complications such as recurrent VTE and the postthrombotic syndrome.
Most patients have one or more risk factors ().

DVT of the upper extremity (UEDVT) is associated with intravascular catheters, strain/trauma, thrombophilic states, and a previous UEDVT. Up to 3% of peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC) may be associated with DVT.

Patients with active cancer have a higher risk of VTE. Idiopathic (unprovoked) DVT may be a sign of malignancy or thrombophilia. However, in one large series only 1 in 146 patients with idiopathic DVT had cancer, and 40% of those were metastatic, which is of little benefit to diagnosis.
Patients undergoing elective knee arthroscopy have a low rate of symptomatic VTE.

Centrally inserted CVCs are associated with a 3% risk of serious complications including DVT (2.7 per 1000 catheter days). Risks associated with insertion can be decreased by using ultrasonography guidance.

Vascular endothelial injury promotes platelet adhesion, resulting in a hemostatic plug, which activates the coagulation pathway. This is normally opposed by flow dilution and circulating anticoagulants and thrombolytics.

DVT results when there is vascular endothelial injury, venous flow stasis, or a hypercoagulable state (Virchow's triad) that cause the physiologic thrombotic process to predominate over the thrombolytic.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Major orthopedic, spinal cord, or general surgery
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT), oral contraceptives (OCPs), pregnancy, or post-partum
Bed rest or immobility due to sitting

list.listitem: Assess each medical and surgical patient for the risk of developing VTE and institute appropriate thromboprophylaxis (see Table 1 in Pulmonary Embolism topic).A
Do not screen routinely for asymptomatic DVT since it is not cost effective and has not been demonstrated to improve outcomes.A
Routine screening for asymptomatic DVT has not been supported by large studies and is not recommended.

Follow American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) guidelines for prophylaxis in at-risk patients (see Table 1 in Pulmonary Embolism topic). Universal prophylaxis is not recommended but should be based on physician judgment and patient risk for VTE.
Padua prediction score (PPS) is a proven model for the assessment of VTE risk in hospitalized medical patients and is associated with reduced VTE incidence when compared with clinical judgement.

Options for VTE prophylaxis include pharmacologic (subcutaneous heparin, LMWH, or fondaparinux) and mechanical measures (graduated compression stockings, intermittent compression devices, and venous foot pumps).

For medical inpatients at moderate or high-risk, consider prophylaxis with LMWH, UFH, or fondaparinux. If choosing UFH, 5000 U three times a day dosing results in 10 fewer PEs, 20 fewer DVTs, and 4 more major bleeds per 10,000 patient days than twice a day dosing. UFH is preferred in patients with low GFR.
One study found Dalteparin 5000 IU daily no more effective than UFH 5000 U twice daily for the prevention of proximal lower extremity DVT in ICU patients.

In high-risk surgical and orthopedic patients, consider LMWH, UFH, or fondaparinux. One study found that fondaparinux was more effective than enoxaparin in patients undergoing major orthopedic surgery. Continue prophylaxis for 4 weeks in cancer patients undergoing surgery. In patients undergoing hip replacement, 21 days of thromboprophylaxis is more effective than shorter course (with a higher risk of minor bleeding). Enoxaparin appears to be superior to aspirin for VTE prophylaxis after total hip arthroplasty or total knee replacement.

Moderate quality evidence supports extended duration anticoagulation (up to 35 days) to prevent VTE post-hip replacement surgery, but risk of minor bleeding is increased. Further evidence is needed regarding extended prophylaxis for knee replacement or hip fracture repair.
In patients having undergone abdominal or pelvic surgery, continuation of LMWH for at least 14 days was found to reduce the risk of VTE.
Once daily LMWH is equally as effective as BID dosing in reducing the incidence of DVT.

Non-pharmacolgoic management with external pneumatic compression is preferred in patients undergoing neurosurgical or urologic surgery because of the increased risk if bleeding occurs, and as an adjunct to anticoagulation treatment in other surgical procedures. In one study, a mobile compression device was similar to LMWH in preventing DVT after hip replacement surgery. However, it had methodologic flaws, and more evidence is needed. Data regarding prophylaxis using anticoagulants following abdominal aortic surgery are lacking.
Other studies have demonstrated that pneumatic compression is more effective than compression stockings, similar in efficacy to medical prophylaxis, and may be safer than anticoagulation.
In one study of ICU patients, there was found to be no benefit with addition of intermittent pneumatic compression to pharmacologic anticoagulation in the prevention of proximal DVTs.

There is high-quality evidence that graduated compression stockings (GCS) are effective in reducing the risk of DVT in hospitalized surgical patients (general and orthopedic surgery), with or without other methods of background thromboprophylaxis, and moderate-quality evidence that GCS probably reduce the risk of proximal DVT. However, it is unknown whether GCS are effective in reducing the risk of DVT in medical patients. GCS are also effective at reducing asymptomatic DVT and edema in airline passengers on long flights.Combining intermittent pneumatic leg compression with pharmacologic prophylaxis reduces the incidence of DVT and PE.
Compression stockings when added to anticoagulation aids in reducing venous thromboembolic events but interestingly does not affect the prevalence of DVT.
Novel oral anticoagulant rivaroxaban was no more effective but was more likely to cause bleeding when compared to enoxaparin in the prevention of VTE in medical inpatients.

Apixaban therapy in patients with active cancer undergoing chemotherapy prevented DVT when compared to placebo (NNT = 17 at 6 months; NNH = 59 from bleeding); rivaroxaban therapy in a similar group of patients failed to show benefit, but discontinuation rates were high and more studies are needed.
Rosuvastatin slightly reduced the risk of VTE in older adults, but only for DVT and not for PE, and at a very high cost (at least $127,400 per DVT prevented). It is not recommended for this purpose.
Peripherally inserted central catheters increase the risk for upper and lower extremity DVT, at a rate of 4.8 per 1000 catheter days.
Single prophylaxis strategies (i.e., rivaroxaban, LMWH) are more effective in prevention of DVT in elective total knee replacment than combination strategies, with rrivaroxaban being most effective.
Low-dose aspirin alone may be of similar efficacy as direct oral anticoagulant therapy in preventing DVT in patients after total knee replacement.

LMWH is safer and more effective than oral anticoagulation at preventing recurrent thromboembolism in patients with cancer. There is no mortality benefit, however, in using LMWH compared with oral anticoagulation in this population.

In patients with cancer needing anticoagulation, consider LMWH, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban for at least 6 months for long-term anticoagulation over vitamin K antagonists (i.e., warfarin). VKAs may be considered if LMWH or DOACs are not available.

A trial randomized 1766 patients with active cancer and a segmental PE or proximal DVT to apixaban in full or low dose. After 6 months of full-dose anticoagulation, a lower dose of apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) provides a similar benefit and less bleeding risk than full-dose apixaban (NNT = 28).
Beyond 6 months, offer anticoagulation with LMWH, DOACs, or VKAs for those with active cancer, such as those with metastatic disease or receiving chemotherapy.

DOACs were more effective than LMWH to prevent recurrent VTE but also associated with increased risk of major and minor bleeding. Risk difference was small (2-3%) for both recurrent VTE at 6 months and major bleeding which may reflect better compliance with DOACs.
Consider indefinite anticoagulation in patients with recurrent VTE, VTE with multiple ongoing risk factors, or a persistently abnormal D-dimer test after treatment.

Evidence is currently insufficient concerning the effectiveness and safety of extended thromboprophylaxis in prevention of recurrent VTE after initial oral anticoagulation in patients with, non-cancer, unprovoked VTE.

Patients with Factor V Leiden mutation are at increased risk of recurrence, but there is no evidence that testing family members improves clinical outcomes. There is no increased risk of VTE with prothrombin G20210A mutation.

Aspirin at 100 mg daily reduces the risk of recurrent VTE by 42% in patients with first unprovoked VTE, without significant bleeding risk increase. NNT of 42 to prevent 1 recurrence. Current ACCP CHEST Guidelines recommend the use of aspirin over no aspirin in those with unprovoked proximal DVT who are stopping anticoagulation therapy.
Extended anticoagulation with warfarin was similar to dabigatran in the prevention of recurrent VTE.
Sulodoxide has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrent DVT in those treated for an unprovoked clot; its superiority to aspirin has not been proved.

DOACs should be used with caution in patients with Antiphospolipid Syndrome as rivaroxaban showed a higher risk of thrombosis and bleeding events in patients when compared to warfarin for treatment of DVT recurrence.
No single clinical feature effectively rules DVT in or out, but the presence or absence of certain clinical features increases or decreases the likelihood of DVT.A
Use a validated clinical decision rule () to establish pretest probability before diagnostic testing.A
A diagnosis of DVT can be confirmed by venography, duplex Doppler ultrasonography, or impedence plethysmography, but the primary diagnostic tool is the ultrasound.A
A normal D-dimer test or a normal result on ultrasound excludes DVT when combined with a low pretest probability.A

list.listitem: Individual findings that best rule in DVT when present are a global MD estimate of high likelihood for DVT, history of malignancy, and history of immobilization or recent surgery.
Findings that best rule it out when absent include global MD estimate of low likelihood, absence of edema, and absence of unilateral calf swelling.
No single clinical feature effectively rules out DVT, so use a validated clinical decision rule.

Use a validated clinical decision rule () to estimate a pretest probablity of DVT, which in turn informs interpretation of diagnostic tests. The Dutch Primary Care rule performs similarly to the Wells prediction rule.

A negative D-dimer test is useful to rule out DVT in patients at low risk for DVT. For older patients (age >50), use of an age-adjusted D-dimer is appropriate in ruling out DVT. The recommended adjustment is by the formula (patient's age x 10) uq/L.
A Dutch study in 2169 non-high risk ED patients with suspected VTE found no patients with VTE who had a d-dimer between 500 and their age adjusted cutoff, and 7.3% fewer imaging studies.

Ultrasonography is the noninvasive test of choice for the diagnosis of proximal DVT in most patients with moderate to high pre-test probability. The accuracy varies according to whether one is looking for any DVT in a symptomatic patient,any DVT in an asymptomatic patient, or proximal DVT in a symptomatic or asymptomatic patient. An RCT of 2098 patients with first episode of DVT compared immediate whole leg Doppler ultrasound with a strategy of ultrasound of the proximal vein only, followed by repeated testing if d-dimer was abnormal. There was no difference outcomes, so this less costly strategy is an acceptable alternative.
Impedance plethysmography with serial studies is an acceptable alternative if ultrasound is not available or if recurrent DVT is a consideration.

Magnetic resonance direct thrombus imaging is as accurate as venography for the diagnosis of DVT, but its routine use is limited by the lack of outcome data and cost. It may be considered if the ultrasound is equivocable, if ultrasound and plethysmography are not available, or if venography is contraindicated in a patient with contrast allergy.
Venography is performed only when the noninvasive tests are unavailable, are nondiagnostic, or are discordant with a high clinical suspicion.
The need for diagnostic testing to detect genetic mutations such as Factor V Leiden is unclear at this time.
Routine abdominal and pelvic CT imaging does not advantage over a basic screening protocol to detect occult malignancy in patients with unprovoked DVT.
The Wells score () integrates the best independent predictors and helps estimate the likelihood of DVT.
It has been well validated in a variety of populations of nonpregnant adults and is a key part of diagnostic algorithms but may not be as helpful in hospitalized patients .
Separate clinical rules for recurrence of DVT in men and women have been developed.
The HERDOO2 risk score predicts recurrence in women.

A novel clinical decision rule for outpatients has been developed and validated in Dutch primary care patients; only 7 of 495 low risk patients had a VTE diagnosed in the subsequent 3 months to their presentation.
The VTE-BLEED risk score predicts the risk of major bleeding in patients with VTE who have been anticoagulated.

Risk scores are less helpful in hospitalized patients. A multicenter study evaluated risk scores in 1273 patients and concluded that the Padua, IMPROVE, and NICE risk assessment models all perform poorly in identifying hospitalized patients at high risk for VTE.
See algorithm in .
If the D-dimer is negative and the patient has a low Wells score () DVT is ruled out. If the D-dimer is negative but patient has moderate or high risk of DVT, order a duplex ultrasound.
Patients who are D-dimer positive should have an ultrasound performed and if positive, initiate treatment. If the US is negative, a repeat US should be done in 3 to 7 days.

Current guildelines suggest that apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban are the preferred drugs for treatment of venous thromboembolism. Alternatively, treat patients with warfarin and UFH or LMWH for at least 5 days and discontinue heparin when the INR has stabilized between 2 and 3.A
LMWH and UFH can both be given subcutaneously.A
Outpatient treatment of DVT is as efficacious and safe and more cost effective compared with inpatient treatment for clincally stable patients.A
The duration of treatment depends on whether a cause is identified and in some cases should be indefinite. See Table 2 in Pulmonary Embolism topic.A

For patients with acute isolated distal DVT and no risk factors for extension, the ACCP guidelines recommend 2 weeks of serial imaging, with anticoagulation only if it extends or if the patient has severe symptoms or develops risk factors for extension.A
See for an overview of anticoagulants for acute DVT.

ACCP guidelines (2021) suggest that direct oral anticoagulants (DOAs) apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban are he preferred treatement for acute DVT. In patients who can only take warfarin, initial anticoagulation should be in the form of LMWH or UFH. LMWH is as effective as UFH for treatment of DVT and is safer (major hemorrhagic complications: LMWH 1.0% vs. UFH 2.1%). It can be administered in fixed doses and does not require laboratory monitoring.
While no longer first line these agents are still an option, especially in low resource settings.

If UFH is used, monitor doses to achieve therapeutic levels (an activated partial thromboplastin time [aPTT] of 1.5-2.5 times control) within the first 24 hours to reduce chance of recurrence. A single study of 708 adults with VTE (mostly DVT) found that high-dose subcutaneous UFH (initial dose of 333 U/kg, followed by a fixed dose of 250 U/kg every 12 hours) was as effective and safe as LMWH. A systematic review identified 15 RCTs with 3054 participants confirming non-inferiority, although with non-significant trends favoring SC LMWH or IV UFH.

Start warfarin simultaneously with heparin (LMWH or UFH); continue both until a therapeutic INR (2-3) is seen for 2 days. Protocols have been developed using 10- or 5-mg starting doses that result in more rapid and accurate anticoagulation. A "gentler" protocol has been designed for use in the elderly. Pharmacogenetic information does not add significant benefit to warfarin dosing algorithms.
Consider at home, point-of-care INR testing and self-adjustment of VKA dose if patient is competent and can afford home monitor.
INR testing intervals should be 4 weeks or fewer following dose adjustments and 4-12 weeks during periods of stable INR control.
Monitor routinely for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (every other day) while the patient is on a heparin product.
ACCP guidelines (2021) suggest that direct oral anticoagulants (DOAs) apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban are he preferred treatement for acute DVT.
NICE guidelines (2020) recommend apixaban or rivaroxaban as initial choices.

The oral agent rivaroxaban (Xarelto) was similarly effective to warfarin in the chronic treatment of DVT. A randomized trial with 3449 participants found less recurrent thromboembolism (2.1% vs. 3.0%; NNT = 111) and no difference in episodes of major bleeding between rivaroxaban and warfarin. Rivaroxaban has also be shown to be effective in the treatment of pulmonary embolus. Prolonged rivaroxaban therapy after intial treatment period for DVT is associated with a reduced risk of recurrent clot (NNT=30-33 at 12 months) relative to aspirin alone.127 Another oral agent, dabigatran (Pradaxa) was compared to warfarin in 2539 patients with venous thromboembolism; there was no difference in the risk of recurrent VTE or major bleeding. Both drugs are much more expensive than warfarin (up to $400/month), but INR testing is not required.
Apixiban is a novel oral anticoagulant (factor Xa inhibitor) that is as effective as warfarin in VTE with a small benefit in major bleeding risk (NNT = 83) but higher cost.

A study in Canada randomized 2709 patients with acute VTE to apixabann or rivaroxaban for 3 months. For the primary outcome of clinically relevant bleeding during the 3-month trial period, the apixaban group fared better (3.3% vs 7.1%; RR 0.46; 95% CI 0.33 - 0.65, NNT = 26). The apixaban group also had a lower risk of major bleeding (0.4% vs 2.4%; RR 0.16; 0.06 - 0.40, NNT = 50). There were no significant differences detected in recurrent symptomatic VTE or all-cause mortality.

In a randomized trial of 600 adults with symptomatic cVTE and at least one ongoing risk factor (BMI >= 30, chronic inflammatory disease, or chronic lung disease), 12 months of apixaban was superior to 3 months. The likelihood of symptomatic recurrent VTE was significantly lower in the apixaban group (1.3% vs 10.0%; P < .001; NNT = 11). Major bleeding occurred in 1 patient in the apixaban group and none in the placebo group; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was numerically more common with apixaban (4.8% vs 1.7%; P = .06).

For cancer associated VTE, an RCT with 1766 patients found that low dose apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) was non-inferior to standard dose apixaban (5 mg twice daily). The primary outcome of recurrent VTE did not differ between groups (2.1% for low dose and 2.8% for full dose; P < .001 for noninferiority). Clinically relevant bleeding was somewhat less likely in the low-dose group (12.1% vs 15.6%; P =.03; NNT = 28).

Edoxaban is another novel oral anticoagulant recently shown to be no less effective and safe as warfarin in VTE, but at a higher cost. In a study that randomized 8240 adults with acute VTE to edoxaban or warfarin, there was no difference in the likelihood of first recurrent VTE, major bleed, or death.
Ask patients about concurrent aspirin use, which is not recommended and greatly increases the risk of major bleeding. A population-based cohort study found this to be a relatively common practice.

A trial randomized 600 adults with a provoked DVT or PE and at least one ongoing risk factor (obesity, chronic inflammatory disease, or chronic lung disease) to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for 3 or 12 months. The likelihood of symptomatic recurrent VTE was significantly lower in the apixaban group (1.3% vs 10.0%; P < .001; NNT = 11). Major bleeding occurred in 1 patient in the apixaban group and none in the placebo group; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was numerically more common with apixaban (4.8% vs 1.7%; P = .06).
Thrombolysis increases patency of veins in proximal DVT, but patient selection is important to minimize the risk of bleeding.
Consider adjuvant catheter-directed thrombolysis in select patients with iliocommon femoral DVT, symptoms <14 days, and life expectancy >1 year if done at an experienced center.

ACCP guidelines (2021) recommend serial imaging for 2 weeks over immediate anticoagulation for patients with isolated distal lower extremity DVT who do not have risk factors for extension or severe symptoms. Anticoagulation is not recommended if the clot is stable and does not extend.

listitem.strong: Patients with active cancer and DVT

list.listitem: A study found DOACs to be noninferior to LMWH for preventing recurrent VTE over a 6-month follow-up in adults with cancer. The 671 participants were randomized to the DOAC of choice or LMWH of choice. Severe adverse events, including major bleeding, occurred similarly in both groups. Outcomes remained similar regardless of specific cancer thrombogenic risk. Patients given DOACs were significantly more likely to still be taking their assigned anticoagulant at 6 months, suggesting a superior outcome with DOACs with longer follow-up.

A trial randomized 1766 patients with active cancer and a segmental PE or proximal DVT to apixaban in full or low dose. After 6 months of full-dose anticoagulation, a lower dose of apixaban (2.5 mg twice daily) provides a similar benefit and less bleeding risk than full-dose apixaban (NNT = 28).
LMWH can be used for long-term therapy if oral anticoagulation is contraindicated or unavailable. It is more effective than warfarin for patients with VTE and comorbid cancer.
Tinzaparin is no better than warfarin in preventing recurrent DVT in patients with cancer.
Manage patients on long-term anticoagulation who need to undergo surgical procedures according to their thromboembolic risk.
For patients on long-term anticoagulation who need to undergo minor procedures, a brief (<5 days) interruption of warfarin therapy is associated with a low risk of thromboembolism.

If high stroke risk, recent VTE, or high risk mechanical heart valve, bridge with LMWH bid 3 days prior to surgery with last dose given 24 hours before surgery. Resume LMWH 48-72 hours post-surgery along with warfarin.
Consider continuing anticoagulation without interuption for minor procedures like cataract surgery, dermatologic procedures or dental procedures.

For patients on rivaroxaban, apixaban or edoxaban, stop 1 day prior to procedures with low bleeding risk and 2 days prior to those procedures with high risk of bleeding. Resume DOAC 1 day after low bleeding risk procedures and 2 days after high bleeding risk procedures.

For those on dabigatran, for low bleeding risk procedures, stop 1 day prior to procedure if creatinine clearance (CrCl) is >50, or 2 days prior if CrCl is <50. For high bleeding risk procedures stop 2 days prior to procedure if CrCl >50 and 4 days prior if CrCl< 50. Resume dabigatran at same number of days used for discontinuation.

Consider external, intermittent pneumatic compression (EPC or IPC) as an alternative in patients who have a high risk of bleeding. Do not use in patients with overt ischemia or in those who have been at bed rest for more than 72 hours without DVT prophylaxis.
Reserve systemic thrombolytics for patients who are hemodynamically unstable or who have massive iliofemoral thrombosis and a low risk for bleeding.

Inferior vena cava (IVC) filters are recommended only when there is an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. IVC filter placement decreases initial PE risk but increases long-term recurrent DVT risk by almost twofold without conferring any difference in long-term symptomatic PE or mortality. A recent cohort study suggests that DVT filters may often be implanted in clinical practice without these clear indications. Current CHEST Guidelines recommend against using an IVC filter in those treated with anticoagulation.
Compression stockings are not more effective than placebo stockings in preventing post-thrombotic syndrome.
Compression stockings have not been shown to reduce the risk of recurrent DVT.
There may be sufficient protection from DVT in post total knee replacement patients with aspirin alone versus anticoagulation.
For isolated distal (below the knee) acute DVT of the leg without severe symptoms or risk factors for extension, consider serial US imaging of deep veins for 2 weeks instead of anticoagulation.
Treat DVT due to transient risk factors for thromboembolic disease or due to surgery for at least 3 months.
Treat first-episode idiopathic DVT for at least 3 months, which may be continued longer if the patient has an elevated D-dimer 1 month after stopping anticoagulation.
Treat indefinitely recurrent DVT, patients with more than one idiopathic event, and patients with cancer.A

In all instances, consider longer treatment with anticoagulation and weigh it against the bleeding risk. There is mounting evidence for the benefits of longer duration of treatment of idiopathic DVT. The likelihood of mortality due to recurrent VTE is higher than that due to fatal bleeding (8%-9% vs. ~2%).
See Table 2 in Pulmonary Embolism topic for suggested duration of treatment.
Hospitalize all patients who are clinically unstable, have cardiovascular or pulmonary comorbidities (especially CHF), or who have contraindications to anticoagulation.
Consider hospitalization if close follow-up is not possible, for those who are pregnant or morbidly obese or who have renal failure or cancer.
Also consider hospitalization in severe, proximal thrombosis (thrombosis above the groin with severe edema of the entire leg).
Postthrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome (chronic dependent edema, pain, skin changes including discoloration) occurs in about 28% of patients after 5 years.

Though earlier unblinded studies showed that compression stockings decreased the incidence and severity of postthrombotic syndrome by 50%; more recent studies have shown no proven benefit in using compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.The most recent CHEST Guidelines no longer recommend their use.

Although HIT was thought to occur more often with UFH than LMWH, a systematic review found that the risk was similar (1.2% for LMWH; 1.5% for UFH). Anticoagulation can be continued with a direct thrombin inhibitor (lepirudin [Refludan]). Warfarin can be restarted once the platelets return to normal.
For bleeding issues, American Society of Hematology (ASH) recommends temporary cessation of VKA (i.e., warfarin) alone without addition of vitamin K when INR is > 4.5 but < 10, and bleeding is minor.

For major bleeding issues, ASH recommends using 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrates (PCCs) over fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) in addition to cessation of VKA agent and IV vitamin K; for major bleeding with LMWH or UFH, use protamine in addition to cessation of LMWH or UFH; for major bleeding with dabigatran, use idaricizumab in addition to cessation of dabigatran; for major bleeding with a DOAC, use either 4-factor PCC or recombinant coagulation factor Xa or inactivated-zhzo in addition to DOAC cessation. ASH notes that these recommendations are based on very low certainty evidence.
The prognosis for most patients with DVT treated with heparin and oral anticoagulants is excellent.A
Fatal PE and recurrent DVT are rare in patients who have transient risk factors and are adequately treated with anticoagulation.A
Most DVTs start in the calf, are asymptomatic, and resolve spontaneously.
Symptomatic calf DVTs extend to the proximal veins approximately 25% of the time in untreated individuals, usually within 1 week of presentation.
Patients with untreated, symptomatic proximal DVT have a PE about 30% to 50% of the time.
Untreated patients with symptomatic proximal DVT or PE have an approximately 50% chance of recurrence within 3 months.
About one-fourth of patients go on to develop the postthrombotic syndrome within 5 years.

The risk of recurrence of VTE associated with transient risk factors is less than 3% a year, whereas patients with idiopathic VTE or those with persistent risk factors have an approximately 10% a year or higher recurrence rate after anticoagulation is stopped.
The risk for fatal PE after a 6-month course of anticoagulant therapy is low (<1%), especially if initial VTE was provoked.

A study of 646 patients with initial unprovoked VTE found that key risk factors for recurrence in women include hyperpigmentation, edema or redness of either leg, abnormal d-dimer, BMI greater than or equal to 30 kg/m2, and age of 65 years or older. For men, risk factors included hyperpigmentation, edema or redness, and an antiphospholipid antibody level greater than 6 U/mL.

A study of 153 patients with an initial episode of acute DVT (about half unprovoked, none with cancer, short life expectancy, or need for permanent anticoagulation) found that 26% had a recurrence during the next 5 years. Factors associated with recurrence were DVT in both proximal and distal veins, unprovoked DVT (RR 2.9) and age over 65 years (RR 1.5). About a quarter had a subsequent PE, and about 1/4 of these events were fatal.

Of patients completing treatment following a first unprovoked VTE, one 2019 meta-analysis showed that approximately 1 in 10 will have a second VTE over the next 12 months, and 4 in 10 will have a second VTE over 10 years. They are also at higher risk of developing a DVT.

Educate patients about signs of bleeding (pink urine, rectal bleeding, black stools, hemoptysis), recurrent DVT, and PE (dyspnea upon exertion, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, tachycardia, anxiety).
Inform patients taking warfarin of drug-drug interactions before starting a new medication and of the importance of laboratory monitoring.
Warfarin crosses the placenta; do not use in pregnant patients.
Use LMWH or UFH, as neither crosses the placenta. As systematic review found no RCTs of anticoagulant treatment in pregnant women with VTE.
A systematic review also found limited data regarding prophylaxis in pregnant women.
Left leg pain, increased calf circumference, and being in the first trimester are useful for diagnosing DVT in pregnant women.

The Kids-DOTT study treated all children with DVT and PE and a provoking risk factor for 6 weeks. At 6 weeks, all patients underwent repeat imaging. Those patients (n = 417) with venous flow occurring in the involved vessel segments and without persistent antiphospholipid antibodies randomly received assignment to either discontinue anticoagulant therapy or to continue anticoagulant therapy for a total of 3 months. Both recurrent VTE and bleeding occurred less often in the 6 week treatment group.

feature.caption: Wells Prediction Rule for Diagnosing Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT).*
feature.feature_body:
Sign or Symptom Score
Active cancer (treatment ongoing or within previous 6 months or palliative) 1
Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremities 1
Recently bedridden for more than 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks that required general or regional anesthesia 1
Localized tenderness along the distribution of the deep venous system 1
Entire leg swollen 1
Calf swelling 3 cm larger than the asymptomatic side (measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity) 1
Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg 1
Collateral superficial veins (nonvaricose) 1
Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT −2
*Probability of DVT is low if score is 0 or less; intermediate if 1 or 2; and high if 3 or more. Adapted from Wells PS, Anderson DR, Bormanis J, et al. Value of assessment of pretest probability of deep-vein thrombosis in clinical management. Lancet 1997;350:1795–1798.

feature.caption: Treatment Options for Patients With Acute Venous Thromboembolism.
feature.feature_body:
Drug Dose Comment
Unfractionated heparin (IV) Initial dose of 80 U/kg and then adjusted based on aPTT (often 18 U/kg/hr continuous IV infusion); aPTT 1.5-2.5 control
Unfractionated heparin (SC) Initial dose of 333 U/kg, followed by a fixed dose of 250 U/kg q12h; alternatively, 8000-10000 U subcutaneously every 8 hours or 15000-20000 U subcutaneously bid. Similarly effective to LMWH in one study
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h or 1.5 mg/kg SC once daily; maximum dose 180 mg/d. If CrCl < 30: reduce dosage to 1 mg/kg once daily Primarily renally cleared
Warfarin Initially 5-10mg po once daily; consider lower dose for older or malnurished patients or those with a higher bleeding risk or liver failure. Start on same day as heparin/LMWH/fondaparinux and bridge for at least 5 days until INR >/= 2 for 24 hours. No renal dosing adjustment needed
Dalteparin 100 U/kg SC q12h or 200 U/kg SC once daily; maximum dose 18,000 U/d. If CrCl < 30: monitor anti-Xa levels Primarily renally cleared
Fondaparinux 5 mg subcutaneously daily (Wgt <50 kg); 100% renal clearance
7.5 mg subcutaneously daily (Wgt 50-100 kg);
10 mg subcutaneously daily (Wgt > 100 kg).
If CrCl 30-50: use with caution; If CrCl < 30: use alternative agent.
Idraparinux Once weekly Effective for DVT but not PE
Ximelagatran 36 mg orally twice daily Similar to enoxaparin/warfarin May elevate LFTs transiently
Lepirudin Initial dose: 0.4 mg/kg body weight (up to 110 kg) slowly IV, followed by 0.15 mg/kg body weight (up to 110 kg)/h as a continuous IV infusion for 2-10 days or longer if clinically needed Direct thrombin inhibitor, indicated for treatment of patients with HIT
Dabigatran DVT/PE Tx: 150 mg po bid (requires overlap with LMWH 5-10 days); DVT/PE prophylaxis (post-hip replacement): 220 mg po daily for 28-35. If CrCl 15-30: 75 mg po bid, CrCl<15: not defined. Expensive; similar to warfarin in direct comparison study
Rivaroxaban DVT/PE Tx: 15 mg po bid for 3 weeks, then 20 mg once daily; DVT/PE prophylaxis (recurrent or post-operative): 10 mg po daily (if post-op: treat 35 days for hip replacement and 12 days for knee replacement). If CrCl <30, consider alternative agent. Expensive, similar to warfarin in direct comparison study
Apixaban DVT/PE Tx: 10 mg po bid for 1 week, then 5 mg bid; DVT/PE prophylaxis (recurrent or post-operative): 2.5 mg po bid (if post-op: treat 35 days for hip replacement and 12 days for knee replacement). Per manufacturer, for DVT tx or prophylaxis, no dosing adjustment needed for renal impairment/ ESRD. Expensive, similar to warfarin in direct comparison study
Edoxaban 60 mg po once daily (Adults > 60 kg), 30 mg po once daily (Adults </= 30 kg); bridge with LMWH for 5-10 days. If CrCl 15-50: 30 mg po once daily; CrCl < 15: use alternative agent. Expensive, similar to warfarin in direct comparison study
Abbreviations: aPTT, activated partial thromboplastin time; CrCl, Creatinine clearance (mL/min/1.73m2); HIT, heparin-induced immune thrombocytopenia; LFTs, liver function tests; LMWH, low-molecular-weight heparin; PE, pulmonary embolism.
